overview:
Born out of the collapse of the imperial Russian army, the Bolshevik force created by decree in January 1918 was meant to be a volunteer army of politically reliable workers built around the Red Guards. That failed almost immediately — roughly twenty thousand men came forward against a hoped-for three hundred thousand — and Leon Trotsky, as commissar for military affairs, rebuilt it on conventional lines: mass conscription from June 1918, an end to the election of officers, and the recruitment of tens of thousands of former tsarist officers as "military specialists," whose loyalty was secured by attaching political commissars to countersign their orders and, in some cases, by holding their families hostage. By the end of the civil war the army was overwhelmingly peasant in composition, enormous on paper — something over five million enrolled by late 1920 — and much smaller in the field, riddled with desertion and dependent on a mix of amnesties, family welfare and summary punishment to hold together. It defeated the White armies and reconquered most of the old empire's borderlands, but was beaten badly outside Warsaw in 1920 in the war with Poland.

The interwar decades turned an improvised revolutionary force into a modern industrial one, and then nearly wrecked it. Mikhail Frunze's reforms of the 1920s gave the general staff real authority; in the 1930s Mikhail Tukhachevsky and others developed "deep operations," an ambitious theory of mechanised warfare in depth, coordinating tanks, aircraft and airborne troops, that was well ahead of most Western thinking. Then in June 1937 Tukhachevsky and a group of senior commanders were convicted at a closed trial of a fabricated German-funded conspiracy and shot, opening a purge that swept through the command structure over the following two years. The consequences showed in the costly winter war against Finland in 1939–40 and, far more catastrophically, in the German invasion of June 1941, when whole armies were encircled and millions of soldiers were taken prisoner — around two million of whom were dead of starvation, disease and execution in German hands by early 1942.

What followed was one of the most extraordinary recoveries in military history. The army that regrouped behind the Volga absorbed the deep-battle ideas its own state had nearly destroyed, drew on relocated war industry and on Lend-Lease transport and supply, and reversed the war at Stalingrad in the winter of 1942–43 and at Kursk the following July. Traditional ranks and shoulder boards came back in 1943, a deliberate turn from revolutionary symbolism toward Russian military tradition. From 1944 Soviet offensives — Bagration above all, which shattered German Army Group Centre — drove west across eastern Europe to Vienna and Berlin, at a price of some 34 million people mobilised and official military dead of roughly 8.7 million, with higher estimates in circulation. The advance also brought mass rape, looting and deportations in the territories it crossed. In February 1946 the force was renamed simply the Soviet Army, and the revolutionary name it had carried since 1918 was retired.
significance: More than any other single institution, this army decided the outcome of the Second World War in Europe: the great majority of the Wehrmacht was tied down in the east for most of the war, and the great majority of German soldiers who died in the war died fighting it. Its advance in 1944–45 determined where the postwar line in Europe fell, installing Soviet power across half the continent and setting the geography of the Cold War for four decades. It also left a durable institutional model — conscript mass army, political officers alongside commanders, doctrine built on deep mechanised operations — copied by communist states from China to Cuba, and its operational theory was studied closely by NATO planners long after 1946. In Russia the memory remains politically live: 23 February is still a national holiday, and the Great Patriotic War is the central pillar of state historical narrative.
coverage: This is written from general reference and institutional overviews — Wikipedia, Britannica, the 1914-1918-Online encyclopedia's article on the army's founding, and the USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia on the Eastern Front — and the dataset itself holds no events at all beneath this story, so nothing here is anchored to specific mapped places or dates. The record is genuinely uneven rather than merely thin: civil-war strength returns were notoriously inflated, purge figures (commonly cited as 30,000–40,000 officers affected) are still argued over and depend on whether one counts executions, arrests or simple dismissals, and Soviet casualty totals were suppressed or manipulated for decades, with the official 8.7 million military dead sitting below several serious scholarly estimates. Much of what was written about the army before 1991 came either from Soviet official history or from hostile émigré and Cold War sources, and although the archives opened substantially in the 1990s, access has narrowed again since.
